title: Dynamic Memory and Ownership Basics
learningObjectives: Explain dynamic allocation and object ownership.
Pair scalar new/delete and array new/delete correctly.
Prefer standard containers and RAII to raw owning pointers.
Recognize leak, double-delete and dangling-pointer risks.

understand.concept: Dynamic storage can outlive a scope but must have clear ownership. Raw new/delete are error-prone; prefer RAII objects and containers. Avoid mismatched delete forms and leaks.
understand.whyItMatters: Understanding dynamic allocation explains heap lifetime and why modern C++ uses managed ownership.
understand.explain: Match allocation/deallocation and prefer standard containers or smart pointers to manage lifetime automatically.

examples.title: Automatic lifetime
examples.explanation: local is alive during the pointer use; no delete is needed.

examples.title: Avoid manual ownership
examples.explanation: Container manages its allocation and cleanup.

examples.title: RAII file object
examples.code: std::ifstream file(\"input.txt\");\n// file closes when object leaves scope
examples.explanation: RAII object manages resource cleanup; include fstream.

examples.title: Explicit raw allocation and matching release
Raw array allocation (prefer vector)
examples.code: int* p=new int[3]{1,2,3};\n// Use elements while valid, then release exactly once with delete[] p.\n// Prefer std::vector<int> for automatic lifetime management.

practise.guidedTask: For Dynamic Memory and Ownership Basics, draw the object and pointer/reference relationships for every example. Mark owner, target, constness, lifetime, validity of access, and any operation that could invalidate the pointer or reference.
practise.independentTask: Write a focused C++ exercise for Dynamic Memory and Ownership Basics. Demonstrate at least three cases, including a safe usage and a boundary/invalid case explained in comments but not executed. State who owns the resource and when each object/view is valid.
hints: Draw the pointer/reference and its target object.
Mark whether the object is alive and who owns it.
Check nullptr and bounds before access.
Consider invalidation, deletion and scope exit.
Use standard containers or smart pointers when they express ownership more safely.

questions.explanation: Local objects are destroyed when scope exits.
Resource cleanup is managed by object lifetime.
Scalar new pairs with scalar delete.
RAII containers/smart pointers reduce manual cleanup.
